title: Netflix and AMC Global Media Ink $500 Million ‘Walking Dead’ Streaming Deal
full_text: × Skip to main content By Alex Weprin Plus Icon Alex Weprin Senior Editor alexweprin Follow Sign Up View All July 30, 2026 4:06am 'The Walking Dead' Jackson Lee Davis/AMC AMC Global Media and Netflix have inked a major five-year, $500 million global streaming rights deal for The Walking Dead Universe. The deal will bring all six spin-off series to Netflix starting next year, creating a unified destination for the franchise, and it will be non-exclusive, meaning that AMC+ will get the original series for the first time in 2027. AMC announced the deal in connection with its quarterly earnings report Thursday morning. While the original Walking Dead has been on Netflix since 2011, the new five-year deal will also expand the show to new territories, including the U.K., Italy, Australia, New Zealand. Related Stories Movies Zoe Saldaña to Receive Locarno Fest Special Honor Business Opposition Grows to FIFA World Cup Sell-Off Plan The new deal covers some 371 episodes of TV between The Walking Dead , Fear the Walking Dead , The Walking Dead: Daryl Dixon , The Walking Dead: Dead City , The Walking Dead: The Ones Who Live , The Walking Dead: World Beyond and Tales of The Walking Dead , with the shows debuting in different territories as their streaming licenses kick in over the course of next year. “Audiences have discovered and loved The Walking Dead on Netflix for nearly 15 years and the show continues to attract new fans,” said Lori Conkling, vp of licensing at Netflix. “We’re excited to partner with AMC Global Media to continue to expand that access to more audiences around the world and bring the entirety of The Walking Dead Universe to Netflix.” “We are thrilled to expand our long-time partnership with Netflix around The Walking Dead , ” said Kristin Dolan, CEO of AMC Global Media. “This deal creates a global destination for this universe – all shows, all episodes – making the franchise more accessible than ever to fans around the world. In addition, the co-exclusive agreement allows us to bring the original series to AMC+ for the first time early next year. Netflix has been an important partner in making The Walking Dead one of the most successful franchises in the history of entertainment. This agreement is a fantastic result for our companies, for the fans and for this timeless IP.” THR

title: ‘The Walking Dead’ Renewed By Netflix In 5-Year, $500M Co-Exclusive Deal With AMC Global Media

The deal is co-exclusive, enabling the series to also stream on AMC+ starting next year. The 371 episodes of the original series and its six spinoffs will stream on Netflix in the UK, Italy, Australia., New Zealand and other new territories along with the U.S., where it has been (on DVD and online) since 2011. The news broke Thursday morning ahead of AMC Global Media’s second-quarter earnings results. Watch on Deadline The original series premiered on Halloween in 2010, going to run for 11 seasons and provide a company-defining economic engine for AMC Global Media. Originally known as Rainbow Media when it was a division of Cablevision, AMC spun off and had its IPO just a few months before the premiere of The Walking Dead . For Netflix, the renewal comes amid heightened investor scrutiny of engagement on its service. Many of its original titles have seen ratings declines in their second seasons, leading to questions about its competitive position, though it remains a dominant force with industry-low churn and best-in-class technology. When it comes to bringing new relevance to library content, the “Netflix effect” remains a potent phenomenon, and The Walking Dead is a prime example. “Audiences have discovered and loved The Walking Dead on Netflix for nearly 15 years and the show continues to attract new fans,” said Lori Conkling, Vice President of Licensing at Netflix. “We’re excited to partner with AMC Global Media to continue to expand that access to more audiences around the world and bring the entirety of The Walking Dead Universe to Netflix.” “We are thrilled to expand our long-time partnership with Netflix around The Walking Dead,” said Kristin Dolan, CEO of AMC Global Media. “This deal creates a global destination for this universe – all shows, all episodes – making the franchise more accessible than ever to fans around the world. title: San Sebastian Sets 2026 New Directors Lineup
full_text: Skip to main content By Zac Ntim Zac Ntim International Reporter @ZacharyNtim More Stories By Zac ‘Welcome II The Terrordome’ Returns To Cinemas With New Restoration, Ngozi Onwurah Discusses How The Film Was Almost Lost & Plans For Her Next Project ‘Elsinore’ Starring Andrew Scott & Olivia Colman To Open London Film Festival Glen Hansard Dies: Oscar-Winning ‘Once’ Songwriter, Actor & Musician Was 56 View All July 30, 2026 3:53am Billy Lumby's 'Florid' © Florid Limited, British Broadcasting Corporation & Film I Väst 2026. The San Sebastian Film Festival has confirmed the lineup of filmmakers that will participate in the New Directors programme at this year’s festival, which is set to run from September 18 to 26. Scroll down for the full lineup. Filmmakers from Bulgaria, Chile, Germany, Iran, Japan, Kazakhstan, Mexico, Norway, South Korea, Spain, Taiwan, the UK and Ukraine will present their first and second feature films in the New Directors sidebar. The Bad Son (El mal hijo), the debut feature by Jaime Lorente, will open the sidebar. The film’s official synopsis reads: When 11-year-old Ruben’s father mysteriously disappears, the boy has to move in with his grandmother, a woman he barely knows. In a rural setting where time seems to have stood still, the child will learn that family wounds are passed down from one generation to another, and will try to find a way to heal them as he grows. ​ Related Stories Festivals Marion Cotillard New Image & First Sales Unveiled For Nicole Garcia's San Sebastian-Bound 'Milo' News Mike Leigh's 'Tender Loving Care' & Pablo Larraín Series 'My Sad Dead' Among Titles Added To San Sebastian Lineup New Directors will close with Billy Lumby’s debut film Florid . The film follows a young man who struggles to balance his mental problems, medication, and drugs with his musical ambitions. The official synopsis reads: Jamal, who has a diagnosis of schizophrenia, lives in a supported housing block, alongside other people with mental health issues. Frustrated by the side effects of his medication, he stops taking it, making the voices he hears become more frequent and extreme. Increasingly changeable in mood, Jamal builds a friendship with Kyla, another resident. But as the voices become more intense, Jamal must confront the blurred line between reality and past family events to come to terms with his voices. Watch on Deadline San Sebastian announced further titles from its official competition earlier this week. Titles set for the Spanish fest include Mike Leigh’s latest feature Tender Loving Care and My Sad Dead , a new series from Chilean filmmaker Pablo Larraín. My Sad Dead will screen at San Sebastian in its feature-length format. Starring are Mercedes Morán, Dolores Fonzi, and Carolina Álvarez. The project is based on four short stories by Mariana Enríquez, and tells the story of Ema, a woman with the ability to see and hear the dead. Leigh’s Tender Loving Care will arrive at San Sebastian after a showing at TIFF. Marion Bailey, Paul Jesson, Kate O’Flynn, and Alice Bailey Johnson star in the film. No synopsis for Tender Loving Care has been provided on either the San Sebastian or TIFF website. San Sebastian simply describes the film as an “insightful exploration of the contemporary world.” The 2026 New Directors Lineup: El mal hijo / The Bad Son Jaime Lorente (Spain) Country(ies) of production: Spain. Cast: Miguel Ángel Puro, Susi Sanchéz, Hugo Arbués, Óscar de la Fuente, Abel de la Fuente Opening Film When 11-year-old Ruben’s father mysteriously disappears, the boy has to move in with his grandmother, a woman he barely knows. In a rural setting where time seems to have stood still, the child will learn that family wounds are passed down from one generation to another, and will try to find a way to heal them as he grows. ​ Florid Billy Lumby (United Kingdom) Country(ies) of production: United Kingdom – Sweden. Cast: Jonathan Jules, Saskia Chana, Unknown T Closing Film Jamal, who has a diagnosis of schizophrenia, lives in a supported housing block, alongside other people with mental health issues. Frustrated by the side effects of his medication, he stops taking it, making the voices he hears become more frequent and extreme. Increasingly changeable in mood, Jamal builds a friendship with Kyla, another resident. But as the voices become more intense, Jamal must confront the blurred line between reality, and past family events, to come to terms with his voices. Bloques erráticos / Erratics Thomas Woodroffe (Chile) Country(ies) of production: Chile – France – Argentina. Cast: Denis Lavant, Daniel Muñoz Freeing himself after spending a hundred years trapped in a glacier, the ghost of the filmmaker Lucien Castelnau wanders through a futuristic Patagonia, where technological progress clashes with forgotten stories. Unable to rest while his cinematic legacy remains unseen, he crosses a world that has deleted him from its memory, in search of a place in history and of spectators, who can finally bring his lost work back to life. Body of Glass Naëmi Ada (Germany) Country(ies) of production: Germany – France. Cast: Soma Pysall, Elise Tilloloy, Manuel Severin, Younès Boucif After a violent incident with her controlling partner Felix, dancer Tian flees their shared life in Marseille. Isolated and desperate for connection, she infiltrates the grieving circle of a young man she never knew. But as she becomes entangled in their mourning and affection, she hides a dangerous secret at home. When lies, grief and reality collapse into each other, Tian must choose whether to break the cycle. Cute Marlene Emilie Lyngstad (Norway) Country(ies) of production: Denmark – Sweden – Norway. Cast: Jan Gunnar Røise, Gina Jaqueline , Karin Bertling, Kitt Maiken Mortensen, Molly Kirk Rasmussen Troubled by forbidden feelings for his seven-year-old stepdaughter, Richard decides to leave his girlfriend. He retreats to his childhood home to renovate ahead of its sale, but his self-imposed exile is disrupted by the childlike presence of his mother’s caregiver, Stella. He soon discovers her double life as a Lolita camgirl, and the two develop a transgressive surrogate father-daughter relationship. Their constructed reality begins to unravel when the stepdaughter he left behind reaches out. Esta soledad / This Solitude Javier Giner (Spain) Country(ies) of production: Spain. Cast: Oriol Pla, Marina Salas, Gemma Martínez, Kai Etxaniz, Itziar Lazkano Leo and Lorea have loved one another. Maybe they still do. But something in them has broken. After five years, their relationship is done. He looks after his sick father, trapped between responsibility and an emotional void that weighs him down. She, caught up in poorly-paid jobs and personal crises, tries to get her life back on track without really knowing where to begin. They are two bodies, tired and alone, pierced by their precarious situation, by unresolved issues, by the emotional legacy of a generation who always seem to come late to everything: to love, to stability, to maturity, to serenity, to personal satisfaction. ​ Lovers Sleep Alone Massih Parsaei (Iran) Country(ies) of production: Germany. Cast: Pooyesh Frozandeh, Ava Darvishi, Marcel Kohler, Wolfgang Wobéto WIP Europa 2025 Iman has built his life in Berlin around absence. From his family, from Iran, from being known. He fills the silence with work, invented stories, and nights with a man he meets for sex in the park. When his cousin, whom he barely knows, arrives from Tehran for a brief visit, what he left behind quietly finds its way back to him. Morro Rodrigo García Saiz (Mexico) Country(ies) of production: Mexico . Cast: Gustavo Sánchez Parra, Anna Diaz, Ernesto Meléndez Mateo is a small-town vet. Since his son died, he has lived a life of silent routines and nameless guilt. The violence of the place isn’t immediately visible: it sits there, lurking, like a never-ending echo. This fragile balance is broken when Mateo has to heal Morro, the local capo’s injured dog. The animal’s everyday care leads to an unexpected bond: a relationship with neither judgement nor words, that enables Mateo to recover the meaning of life. Mugalim Ayana Nurdinova (Kazakhstan) Country(ies) of production: Kazakhstan. Cast: Oljas Dalelkhan, Rustem Zhanyamanov, Shynar Janysbekova, Olga Landina, Gulnara Dusmatova, Akif Petrov, Madina Yesmanova, Anna Starchenko, Ruslan Duysembekov Zhandos, a music teacher, lives in the small town of Balkhash and dreams of moving to a big city. He is loved by his students, and the school turns a blind eye to his side jobs. When a patron nostalgic for his hometown arrives, Zhandos is given a chance to leave. He must decide what matters more: the art within him, or himself within art. Obuvkite na bashta mi / My Father’s Shoes Hristo Simeonov (Bulgaria) Country(ies) of production: Bulgaria – France. Cast: Valeria Varbanova, Tanya Shahova, Vyara Kolarova Mima has grown up in the shadow of her father’s absence, raised by her uncompromising mother, Boyka. When news of his death arrives, and his body returns to their village, recognition becomes both duty and dilemma. As Boyka refuses to face the man she once loved, mother and daughter confront a silent past, forcing Mima to decide what it means to inherit a life she never chose. Ri Guang / Will You Still Be My Friend Lu Po-Shun (Taiwan) Country(ies) of production: Taiwan – Singapore. Cast: Jaden Wang, Aloysius Looi, Lung Tien Hsiang, Lu Yi-Ching, Andie Chen, Kate Pang Amid an escalating feud in a rural Taiwanese village, a boy struggles to protect his secret friendship with his Singapore-raised best friend as adult conflicts threaten to tear them apart, while he quietly begins to question the true nature of his feelings for his friend. Sieben Tage Februar / February, Seven Days Tatjana Moutchnik (Ukraine) Country(ies) of production: Germany – Austria – Spain. Cast: Serhii Korshykov, Volodymyr Holosniak, Maria Shtofa, Arsenii Markov, Moisej Bazijan, Daria Guitbout WIP Europa 2025 Two different notions of family identity clash when a man from Odesa and his son visit his brother in Germany for the funeral of their mother, the day before the Ukraine war breaks out. The Ballet Lesson Kazuya Murayama (Japan) Country(ies) of production: Japan. Cast: Vadim Bushmakin, Nikita Kondo, Niina Kondo, Yukina Shimizu In a provincial Japanese town, Japanese-Russian siblings Nikita and Nina live an isolated life with their Russian grandparents, knowing their absent parents only through stories. When their father Nikolai suddenly returns, he takes them on a journey to see their mother Yuki, a Japanese ballet dancer. Along the way, the children discover unfamiliar landscapes, brief encounters, and the fragile bonds of family. The World Before Yoon Dan-bi (South Korea) Country(ies) of production: South Korea – Japan – France. Cast: Su-bin Sim, Eo-jin Kim Seventeen-year-old Jin has never left the island where she was born—a place with no road to the mainland, where the sea quietly sets the rhythm of everyday life. When Dujae returns for his grandmother’s funeral, he stays alone in the house she left behind. Jin begins finding small excuses to visit him, and little by little, seeing him becomes part of her everyday life. As summer wears on, the island she has always known begins to feel unfamiliar—the roads, the sea, the faces around her, all subtly transformed. Jin finds herself looking at it, and at herself, for the first time. But summer, like everything else on the island, will not stay. title: Zoe Saldaña to Receive Locarno Fest Special Honor
full_text: × Skip to main content By Georg Szalai Plus Icon Georg Szalai Global Business Editor View All July 30, 2026 3:12am Zoe Saldaña Frazer Harrison/WireImage Zoe Saldaña ( Guardians of the Galaxy , Emilia Pérez , Lioness ) will be among the stars attending the 79th edition of the Locarno Film Festival . On Monday, Aug. 10, she will feature in a special conversation with the public where she will also be awarded a Special Pardo, or Special Leopard honor, organizers said on Thursday. Italian musician Claudio Simonetti ( Suspiria, Dawn of the Dead ), the keyboardist of the progressive rock band Goblin who has specialized in creating the scores for Italian and U.S. horror films since the 1970s, will also be honored “for his legendary contribution to music in film.” He will receive his honor on Thursday, Aug. 6 ahead of a special screening of Cut and Run ( Inferno in diretta ). Jared Leto Denies Criminal Sexual Conduct: “I Have Never Sexually Assaulted Anyone” View All July 30, 2026 3:01am Mark Jermin Management is one of the UK's best-known children’s agents Keagan Henman/Unsplash EXCLUSIVE : Mark Jermin Management, the prominent UK children’s agency, has stripped a clause from some actor contracts that made it “conditional” for clients to train at its sister stage school, potentially breaching UK law. Deadline revealed last week that Mark Jermin Management (MJM), which discovered stars including Heartstopper lead Kit Connor and A Knight of the Seven Kingdoms breakout Dexter Sol Ansell , could have broken UK agency regulations by effectively charging actors training fees for the opportunity to secure representation. In emails seen by Deadline, MJM encouraged young people to attend paid-for acting classes, provided by sister company the Mark Jermin Stage School (MJSS), if they wished to be represented by the agency. In one 2023 email, an MJM representative told a parent that the company “only represents” young actors “who regularly train and attend our classes.” UK law prohibits agencies from charging upfront fees for representing their clients. Watch on Deadline Related Stories News Mark Jermin, TikTok-Famous Agent Who Discovered 'Harry Potter' & 'Wednesday' Stars, May Have Broken UK Agency Law News Everything We Know About The 'Heartstopper' Movie So Far In a statement last week, a spokesperson for MJM founder Mark Jermin strongly denied that representation has “ever been contingent upon the purchase of training services.” Following publication, Deadline obtained a leaked copy of a 2025 MJM representation contract, which raised serious questions about the accuracy of the agency’s statement. The fourth paragraph of the leaked contract reads: “If you have been scouted from Mark Jermin classes or events, this is a conditional offer given with the understanding that you will continue training with Mark Jermin so the agency can monitor your progress and development. You agree to disclose any intention to leave training and discuss this with the agency ahead of any action.” Section of leaked Mark Jermin Management contract Deadline confronted MJM with the contract clause and asked how it was compatible with last week’s statement. A spokesperson said the clause only appeared in a small number of client contracts and was a “recommendation” that was never enforced. The MJM spokesperson added that the clause would be stripped from agreements as part of an ongoing review by an external consultant. Deadline presented the clause to three agency law experts, all of whom said it raised questions about MJM’s denials of unlawful conduct. Adrian Marlowe, a Lawspeed attorney who specializes in agency laws, said it was a “clear breach” of Regulation 5 of the UK Conduct of Employment Agencies and Employment Businesses Regulations 2003, which states that agencies must not make work-finding services conditional upon work-seekers using other services. “Use of phrases such as ‘with the understanding that,’ and ‘so the agency can monitor’ cannot alter the clear condition which comes into effect when the offer is accepted,” he explained. An MJM spokesperson said: “The wording you have identified is confined to a very small number of contracts in our overall database. The majority of clients of both the stage school and MJM do not have this wording in their contracts and, as part of our ongoing work with business consultants, the wording has been removed from all contracts. “The reason for the wording was to enable the team at MJM and the stage school to monitor and assess the actors’ progress in order to gauge their ability and suitability for any roles that they might be put forward for. “In this sense it’s more of a recommendation and the condition was never enforced. No payment was demanded upfront and clients were free to end their association with the stage school while continuing to be represented by MJM without prejudice. A number of clients have opted to discontinue their training and are still represented by MJM.” The source who shared the contract with Deadline said: “These words in the contract were not seen as a ‘recommendation’ … it was seen as ‘conditional,’ as per the wording in the contract.” They added: “These two words have very different meanings.” In a statement last week, Jermin’s spokesperson said that MJM denies “unequivocally allegations of deliberate wrongdoing, unlawful conduct or systemic misconduct. In particular, we strongly reject any suggestion that representation by Mark Jermin Management has ever been contingent upon the purchase of training services.” Jermin is one of the UK’s best-known children’s agents, unearthing talent including Wednesday’s Evie Templeton, Harry Potter series star Eire Farrell, and Iona Bell, who will feature in Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping . He has parlayed his expertise into a significant social media presence, which he uses to promote his management work and market acting lessons, promising to make stars out of young people. title: ‘Ramayana’ Trailer: Ranbir Kapoor and Yash Face Off in First Part of Nitesh Tiwari’s Epic
full_text: Jul 30, 2026 2:53am PT ‘Ramayana’ Trailer: Ranbir Kapoor and Yash Face Off in First Part of Nitesh Tiwari’s Epic By Naman Ramachandran Plus Icon Naman Ramachandran Latest ‘Ramayana’ Trailer: Ranbir Kapoor and Yash Face Off in First Part of Nitesh Tiwari’s Epic 1 hour ago Busan’s Asian Project Market Unveils 30 Selections for 2026 Edition 4 hours ago Thanh Hang, Hong Anh’s Vietnamese Period Drama ‘Madame in Saigon’ Lands North American Rights Deal With Reel Citrus, Live On (EXCLUSIVE) 4 hours ago See All Prime Focus Studios The first trailer for “ Ramayana ” has debuted, marking the most substantial promotional asset yet for Nitesh Tiwari ‘s two-part adaptation of the ancient Hindu epic, ahead of a worldwide release this November. The story follows exiled prince Rama ( Ranbir Kapoor ) and his consort Sita (Sai Pallavi) through exile into catastrophe, as Sita’s abduction at the hands of Ravana ( Yash ) sets in motion an epic war between righteousness and evil. Part 1 is expected to culminate with the abduction itself, leaving the rescue campaign and the climactic battle for Part 2. Both parts are filmed for Imax. The two films together are budgeted at approximately $500 million, Variety understands. Related Stories Anne Hathaway's Oscars 'Odyssey': Will She Campaign for Lead Actress or Supporting? Oscar Voters Rave Over Christopher Nolan's 'The Odyssey' at First Academy Screenings: ‘The Definitive Filmmaker of Our Time’ The long-awaited trailer offers a sweeping first look at the Hindi-language spectacle, which will also be dubbed into several other languages. Popular on Variety The preview opens with an introduction to demon king Ravana asserting his dominion across the three realms of heaven, earth, and the underworld. A voiceover establishes the overarching mythological conflict, explaining how Lord Vishnu takes human form to restore righteousness on earth when chaos threatens the universe, introducing Kapoor’s Prince Rama as King Dasharatha’s (Arun Govil) eldest son. The trailer shifts focus to Rama’s 14-year exile to the forest to uphold his father’s vow, accompanied by his wife Sita and brother Lakshmana (played by Ravi Dubey). The peaceful exile is shattered when Ravana’s sister, Surpanakha (played by Rakul Preet Singh), becomes infatuated with Rama, setting off a chain of events that leads to her humiliation. Vowing retribution, Ravana steps in to restore his pride, initiating the conflict that leads to Sita’s abduction. Building to a grand finale, the footage showcases high-scale visual effects, mythological weaponry, and massive army battles as Rama vows to defeat Ravana across the three worlds and rescue Sita, signaling the start of the era of Rama. The film is produced by Namit Malhotra’s Prime Focus Studios and Yash’s Monster Mind Creations. Kapoor, Yash, Tiwari and Malhotra, founder of Prime Focus and DNEG CEO, appeared at San Diego Comic-Con to debut the new clip and discuss the making of the epic movies. “Ramayana” Part 1 is set to open during the Diwali holiday frame, with Part 2 following on Diwali 2027. The choice of release window is no accident. Diwali – one of the most widely observed festivals in the Hindu calendar – marks the return of Rama to his kingdom of Ayodhya after 14 years of exile and his victory over Ravana. The lighting of lamps that defines the celebration is said to represent the illumination of Ayodhya on the night its beloved prince came home. Score duties are shared by Oscar-winning composers Hans Zimmer and A.R. Rahman. DNEG – the eight-time Oscar winning VFX house, whose credits include the “Dune” movies, “Interstellar” and “Inception” – is handling visual effects. Tiwari, whose “Dangal” remains the highest-grossing Indian film ever made, directs from a screenplay by Shridhar Raghavan. Sony Pictures is handling international distribution for all territories outside India and Dharma Productions within India. title: Opposition Grows to FIFA World Cup Sell-Off Plan
full_text: × Skip to main content By Scott Roxborough Plus Icon Scott Roxborough Europe Bureau Chief sroxborough Follow Sign Up View All July 30, 2026 2:29am FIFA President Gianni Infantino Catherine Ivill - AMA/Getty Images Pushback to a controversial plan put forward by FIFA boss Gianni Infantino to sell off stakes in the World Cup and other commercial operations to private investors is growing. European soccer governing body UEFA has called an emergency meeting of its members on Thursday to discuss a coordinated response to the plan, with a European boycott of FIFA tournaments among the options being discussed. UEFA has condemned Infantino’s proposal, calling it a plan to “sell the soul” of football. Other major regional soccer bodies, including the Asian Football Confederation (AFC) and Concacaf, which covers North and Central America as well as the Caribbean confederations, have also criticized the proposals, saying they were not consulted on the plan and only became aware of it through the media. Related Stories TV Matthew Macfadyen, Claire Foy to Lead Adaptation of David Nicholls Romance 'You Are Here' Movies Locarno Director Touts "Adventurous" Lineup for "Era of Algorithms" and Highlights Theme of Community The plan would see FIFA set up a new entity, called FIFA Forward Enterprise (FFE), that would bundle all the money-making operations associated with the soccer World Cup — including broadcast rights, sponsorship, ticket sales and licensing fees — and sell a significant stake in the new operation to private investors. Thrive Capital, an investment company founded by Joshua Kushner, brother of Donald Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner, is leading the search for investors. FIFA is valuing the FFE at around $20 billion and has said the plan to sell equity stakes in the commercial group could raise an additional $10 billion for its member organizations. Those members, the 211 national soccer associations that make up FIFA, would have to vote to approve the proposal. The opposition by UEFA, Concacaf, and the AFC suggests Infantino could have a fight on his hands. Together, those three confederations make up 143 of the 211 FIFA members. But opposition to the FFE is not a unified front. In Europe, Czechia’s soccer association has backed the plan. Despite the AFC’s disapproval, association member Saudi Arabia is also believed to support it. Saudi Arabia will host the 2024 World Cup and the Saudi soccer association is a close ally of Infantino. It is not clear whether the FIFA plan can pass with a simple majority vote or if the proposal requires a change to FIFA statutes, which necessitates a 75 percent majority. Infantino released a video on Wednesday evening calling the FFE “a proposal, an offer,” that would be subject to a democratic and consultation process. “It is an opportunity but not an ­obligation,” he said. “It is a golden opportunity to turbocharge the development of the game globally.” That “golden opportunity” will come with payments to FIFA members. FIFA has given members until Sept. 19 to decide whether to apply for an initial payment of $20 million from the proposed sell-off. In a statement, UEFA said the $20 million payoff “says everything you need to know about this plan” and accused FIFA of “using our sport to enrich themselves and their friends.” Concacaf and the AFC have not been as sharp in their criticism, but in a statement Concacaf said they were “deeply concerned by the lack of due process,” noting Concacaf “was only made aware of this matter through media reports and, subsequently, via a media release.” The AFC issued a similar statement, saying they were “not consulted on the proposal and [are] disappointed that a matter of such significance entered the public domain before the AFC family had been afforded the opportunity to examine and discuss it through the appropriate and established governance channels. While the AFC recognizes the importance of exploring innovative approaches that can strengthen the future of global football, initiatives of this scale and consequence must be founded upon the principles of good governance, transparency and meaningful consultation.” FIFA is could also face a backlash from elite clubs. The European Football Clubs organization, which represents more than 850 clubs, complained they were also not consulted on the FFE plan. “The EFC learned about this proposal in the same way as most global football stakeholders – without warning and through the media.” UEFA could vote to boycott upcoming FIFA tournaments, including next year’s Women’s World Cup in Brazil, though that is considered an extreme option and could be seen as unduly punishing the women’s game for a proposal which is primarily focused on monetizing the men’s World Cup and men’s Club World Cup. title: Giorgio Armani Series in the Works From Fremantle-Owned Lux Vide and Iconic Designer’s Fashion House (EXCLUSIVE)
full_text: Jul 30, 2026 2:00am PT Giorgio Armani Series in the Works From Fremantle-Owned Lux Vide and Iconic Designer’s Fashion House (EXCLUSIVE) By Nick Vivarelli Plus Icon Nick Vivarelli International Correspondent @NickVivarelli Latest Giorgio Armani Series in the Works From Fremantle-Owned Lux Vide and Iconic Designer’s Fashion House (EXCLUSIVE) 2 hours ago Reply AI Film Festival Unveils Jury Featuring ‘The Lion King’ Director Rob Minkoff, ‘Twilight’ Helmer Catherine Hardwicke and More 2 days ago Venice Chief Alberto Barbera Under Fire for Lack of Female Directors in Competition: ‘It Is a One-Dimensional Selection’ 3 days ago See All Courtesy Armani/Fremantle The life and career of Giorgio Armani is set to be the subject of a high-end TV series produced by Italy’s Lux Vide, which is collaborating with the fashion house founded by the iconic designer known for his close ties to Hollywood. The still-untitled Armani biopic series — which will be tailored for the international market — has enlisted Turkish-born Italy-based director Ferzan Ozpetek , who is known for combining artistic depth with box-office appeal. Related Stories EA's 'Skate.' to Launch X Games-Themed In-Game Event (Gaming News Roundup) Ozpetek, who knew Armani personally, recently scored a global hit with the 2025 crowdpleaser “Diamonds,” about a group of warm-hearted women in a Rome atelier rushing to fulfill a demanding order from an Oscar-winning costume designer client in the 1970s. “Diamonds” scored mightily at the box local office and traveled widely. Ozpetek’s TV experience includes 2022’s first Disney+ Italian original series “The Ignorant Angels,” a romantic drama spun off from his local hit “Ignorant Fairies.” Popular on Variety “I knew, admired and spent time with Giorgio for many years, both on official occasions and in more private settings,” Ozpetek said in a statement to Variety. “We talked about cinema, of which he was notably passionate and an expert. But also about art, costumes, architecture, and, I would say, life itself. I could see within him a visionary and a brilliant artist. But also a down-to-earth and very determined man.” The director added: “The opportunity to tell his story is both an exciting honor and a challenge that involves capturing the many facets of such a complex, original and captivating personality.” Ozpetek is co-writing the screenplay for the Armani series in collaboration with Lux Vide’s head writer Francesco Arlanch, whose credits include Lux’s widely exported series “Medici,” “Hotel Costiera” and medical drama “Doc.” Storylines and series structure are being kept under wraps. Known globally as the Milan-based fashion pioneer with piercing blue eyes and a vision that combined laid back elegance and attention to detail, Armani first made his mark with the unlined men’s sports jackets and deconstructed suits worn by Richard Gere in 1980 in “American Gigolo.” But Armani also reimagined the woman’s power suit. He dressed scores of Hollywood’s female stars including Julia Roberts, Diane Keaton, Jodie Foster, Cate Blanchett, Lupita Nyong’o, Anne Hathaway and Michelle Yeoh in both minimalist attire — such as the Armani men’s suit famously worn by Julia Roberts when she won a Golden Globe for “Steel Magnolias” in 1990 — and glittery gowns like the “Nairobi blue” crystal-encrusted sequin gown worn by Lupita Nyong’o at the 2024 Academy Awards. The long list of male actors who regularly wore Armani on red carpets, and also on screen, comprises Leonardo DiCaprio, George Clooney Russell Crowe, Robert De Niro and Tom Cruise, to name a few. His Hollywood connection earned Armani wardrobe film credits in more than 200 movies. Armani — a self-made man who fully owned his $10 billion fashion empire at the time of his death on Sept. 4, 2025 at age 91 – was known to often appear in dark trousers and his trademark black T-shirt. He was born in the northern Italian town of Piacenza on July 11, 1934. After two decades in the fashion industry starting in 1957, he and his partner Sergio Galeotti sold their Volkswagen for $10,000 to start up their own menswear ready-to-wear label. They launched both men’s and women’s lines the following year. Fiercely private, Armani rarely discussed his personal life. He did tell Vanity Fair that he had romances with both men and women. He was in long-term relationship with Galeotti until his AIDS-related death in 1985. The Giorgio Armani fashion house has agreed to support production of the Fremantle TV series, providing access to its “archives, creations and iconic locations, offering an unparalleled insight into the world and legacy of one of fashion’s most influential figures,” according to a Fremantle statement. “For years, Lux had been chasing the dream of telling the world the story of Giorgio Armani, an artist who invented a unique and recognizeable style,” Lux Vide founder and president Matilde Bernabei said in a statement. She went on to describe Armani as “a standard-bearer of Made in Italy who rewrote the rules of style and elegance.” “It will be an ambitious series,” Bernabei added, “and we are proud to know that the market has immediately embraced this project with interest, enthusiastically confirming its international potential.” Giorgio Armani and Ferzan Ozpetek Stefano Guindani/Courtesy Armani Trumps Received $10.7 Million Fee for Amazon’s ‘Melania’ Documentary Taylor Swift Reveals Original Song for ‘Toy Story 5’: ‘I Knew It, I Knew You’ — a ‘Return to Country’ Lesley Manville Joins Brett Goldstein in Amazon Comedy Series ‘Escorted’ Spike Lee, Adam Sandler, Ben Stiller, Larry David, Timothée Chalamet and More Watch New York Knicks Pull Off Biggest Comeback in NBA Finals History Taylor Swift Performs ‘I Knew It, I Knew You’ at ‘Toy Story 5’ Premiere, Says Movie Is a ‘Masterpiece’ ‘Carrie’ TV Series: First-Look Images From Mike Flanagan’s Take on Stephen King Classic Loading comments... title: Matthew Macfadyen and Claire Foy to Lead Adaptation of David Nicholls’ ‘You Are Here’ for BBC and Starz
full_text: Jul 30, 2026 1:34am PT Matthew Macfadyen and Claire Foy to Lead Adaptation of David Nicholls’ ‘You Are Here’ for BBC and Starz By Alex Ritman Plus Icon Alex Ritman @alexritman Latest Matthew Macfadyen and Claire Foy to Lead Adaptation of David Nicholls’ ‘You Are Here’ for BBC and Starz 2 hours ago Ewan McGregor and Alan Cumming to Lead Scottish Stage Adaptation of Harry Macqueen’s Gay Romantic Drama ‘Supernova’ 19 hours ago Jared Leto Says ‘I Have Never Sexually Assaulted Anyone’ Amid New Allegations: ‘These Claims Are Categorically False’ 19 hours ago See All Josh Wool, Juankr Matthew Macfadyen and Claire Foy are to lead the TV adaptation of “You Are Here,” the bestselling novel by “One Day” author David Nicholls. The 8-part series — which was first announced by Variety earlier this year — has been green lit by the BBC and Starz, with Lenny Abrahamson directing, reuniting with the BBC for the first time since “Normal People.” Set to be filmed around in the Lake District and around Manchester, “You Are Here,” is being produced by the Fremantle-owned Irish powerhouse Element Pictures, who also produced “Normal People.” Global sales will be handled by Fremantle with De Maio Entertainment spearheading the partnership with Starz. Related Stories EA's 'Skate.' to Launch X Games-Themed In-Game Event (Gaming News Roundup) Set along the Coast to Coast walking trail from the Lake District to Robin Hood’s Bay in North Yorkshire, “You Are Here” follows Michael (Macfadyen) and Marnie (Foy), strangers thrown together by a mutual friend who unexpectedly find themselves setting off on an epic walk. title: Mubi to Release ‘La Mesías,’ From ‘La Bola Negra’ Cannes Best Director Winners, in the U.K., Germany, Canada, Australia and Beyond (EXCLUSIVE)
full_text: Jul 30, 2026 1:21am PT Mubi to Release ‘La Mesías,’ From ‘La Bola Negra’ Cannes Best Director Winners, in the U.K., Germany, Canada, Australia and Beyond (EXCLUSIVE) Created by Javier Ambrossi and Javier Calvo, ‘La Mesías’ is hailed by its fans as one of the greatest shows made in Spain in its recent golden age of film and TV By John Hopewell Plus Icon John Hopewell Chief International Correspondent john_hopewell Latest San Sebastián New Directors: Billy Lumby, Marlene Emilie Lyngstad, ‘Money Heist’ Star Jaime Lorente and More 27 minutes ago EFD Studios Names José Miguel Álvarez Ibargüengoitia CEO, EFD Studios Mexico (EXCLUSIVE) 19 hours ago San Sebastián Lineup: Pablo Larraín, Mike Leigh, Benjamín Naishtat and More 2 days ago See All La Mesías Courtesy Mubi “La Mesías,” the multi-prized series created by Javier Ambrossi and Javier Calvo , behind the Cannes best-director winning “ La bola negra ,” will be released by Mubi in U.K., Canada, Turkey, the Netherlands, Germany and Austria and Australia, streaming exclusively from Sept. 3. A Movistar Plus Original, produced in collaboration with Ambrossi and Calvo’s label Suma Content, “La Mesías” will also stream on Mubi in France, Mubi announced Thursday. The deal was closed with Movistar Plus International. Mubi will launch with a two-episode premiere. Related Stories Christopher Nolan's Oscar 'Odyssey': Can Matt Damon, Monsters and Mythology Deliver Another Best Picture Statue? Hollywood Can't Survive Without Animation. So Why Won't the Industry Respect It? A step-up from “Veneno,” which made a splash on HBO in the U.S., six-part series “La Mesías” delivered a example of the full-on ambition of Los Javis, as Ambrossi and Calvo are known in Spain, which was seen again in “La bola negra,” one of the highest-profile Cannes main competition contenders which sparked rave reviews, and a bidding war for the U.S. rights. Popular on Variety “La Mesías,” Los Javis’ title just prior to “La bola negra,” begins with thirtysomething loner Enric watching a viral video of Stella Maris, a Christian pop band. His reaction? He literally wets himself. For the singers are his younger sisters. Memories flood back of his own childhood and youth, traumatized by his parents’ religious fanaticism which climaxes in mother Montse declaring herself the daughter of God, and that the words her daughters sing are dictated to her by God and part of her mission to save humanity via music. Enric escaped. He now determines to save his sisters. Action flashes back and forward from a present-day 2013 to the 1980s when Enric and slightly younger sister Irene are kids, to around 1997, catching them in their late teens. The production shot for 25 weeks totally on location, mostly at 30 rural sites outside Barcelona. The series featured 170 characters and 3,800 extras. 1980s flashbacks are sometimes lensed in 16 mm, capturing the impressionism of memory. The series genre hops: Episode 1 blends psychodrama and sci-fi, for example. Ep. 2 has a procedural pulse; Episode 3 works like a real-life musical. For all its style, the series delivers a powerful sense of the importance of family education. To mark Mubi’s release announcement, it has shared with Variety a new international trailer, which captures Enric (Roger Casamayor, “Pan’s Labyrinth”) as he seeks out sister Irene (Macarena García), literally scarred by the past, to help him rescue his sisters, plus the presentation of an early video, “lyrics by God,” says one little sister, and later bizarre Christian pop rap, created by Spanish underground duo Carlos Ballesteros and Genís Segarra. Rosalía producer Raül Refree composed the series’ original soundtrack. Messianic matriarch Montse is played at different ages by Ana Rujas (“Cardo”), Cannes best actress winner Lola Dueñas (“Volver,” “La bola negra”) and Carmen Machi, star of Series Mania winner “Celeste.” “It’s very difficult to unlearn what you’ve been taught – I’m talking about education – the past resounds in your body for ever. That touches me in many ways. As a son, a member of the LGBT collective. The series talks about religion, but as a form of education and this is what makes it interesting,” Javier Calvo said on a Variety set visit to the isolated family house, hidden in wooded mountains south of Barcelona. “La Mesías” world premiered at San Sebastián Festival in 2023, where it gleaned glowing reviews. It went on to become the first Spanish series to be selected for the Sundance Festival, win direction and a Student Audience Award at Series Mania and, released by Arte France, be hailed by La Liberation as “one of the most beautiful series of the year.” Picked up off Cannes by Netflix, “La bola negra” is now being positioned as an awards contender. title: Locarno Director Touts “Adventurous” Lineup for “Era of Algorithms” and Highlights Theme of Community
full_text: × Skip to main content By Georg Szalai Plus Icon Georg Szalai Global Business Editor View All July 30, 2026 1:00am Giona A. Nazzaro Rosdiana Ciaravolo/Getty Images Attending the 79th edition of the Locarno Film Festival allows you to embark on a cinematic adventure, if you are so inclined and if you desire to do so. After all, there are all sorts of new envelope-pushing and experimental movies to explore. Or you can see the latest from your favorite auteurs. Among others, the 2026 lineup of the Swiss festival will world premiere Nowhere to Lay My Eyes , the new film from South Korean auteur Hong Sangsoo ( Right Now, Wrong Then ), who is a former Golden Leopard winner at the fest, Canadian director Denis Côté’s Nobody’s Violence , and Sixteen Moments of My Life from Spain’s Albert Serra ( Afternoons of Solitude ). Related Stories TV Disney+ Greenlights 'House of Fates,' Spinoff of Hit Korean Fortune-Telling Series 'Battle of Fates' Lifestyle Paul Newman's Daughter Clea on the Charity He Built -- and Why She'll Never Retire From It Plus, there are screen classics, such as Martin Scorsese’s Taxi Driver and David Lynch’s Wild at Heart , plus a 4K restored version of the extended director’s cut of Kevin Costner’s Dances With Wolves . Of course, Locarno will also feature star power, with 2026 fest honors set to be bestowed upon directors James Gray and Darren Aronofsky , Belgian-born actress Virginie Efira , Rick Baker, the seven-time Oscar winner behind some of cinema’s most fantastical creatures , as well as actresses Asia Argento and Isabella Rossellini . Locarno artistic director Giona A. Nazzaro , who put together the lineup for Locarno79 with his team, spoke to The Hollywood Reporter about underlying and overarching themes that audiences may notice across the program, actors as “living history of cinema,” and allowing people to be surprised and experience a sense of wonder in the age of algorithms. When you unveiled this year’s festival lineup, you called the program “adventurous.” Can you explain a little bit why that seemed such a fitting way to describe the lineup? Adventurous is the adjective that describes the experience that I was always looking forward to when I myself was visiting festivals as a cinephile or a journalist. I really wanted to explore cinema, and therefore I would go to wildly different festivals. And that is probably the reason why I’m here at Locarno today in this position. Locarno was always the festival that allowed me to be in different places at the same time. For instance, if I were to go to Venice, I would see this kind of cinema. If I were to go to Cannes, I would see that kind of cinema, and so on. For me, in a place like Locarno, you have this opportunity that if you don’t care about just a certain kind of film, you can flesh out a program where you can follow your whims and desires and inclinations, but on the other hand, if you want to explore, you can also do that. Today, in the era of algorithms that try to foresee what you will do in a week or so, simply because you clicked on a link and you read something, and then suddenly, in your feeds, this thing keeps on appearing. I wanted to create an algorithm-free experience where you can discontinue the expectations that you might have on your own behalf and push you into a situation where you can experience something else. I know this sounds very aloof, but it goes back to the possibility of being surprised, the possibility of wonder. You see a film, and you say, “Oh my God, what did I just see?” And that does not mean that you have to like it. But for me, if you are taken out of the set of conventions that usually inform your choices, that is a reward in itself. I know this also comes from a privileged point of view. I have the privilege of working with an artistic selection committee that is incredibly talented, and with our privileged viewpoint, with our gaze, we really embrace a wide spectrum of possibilities. This year’s Locarno awards go to big names again, and the lineup also features some bold names, such as Caleb Landry Jones. How do you think about the need for stars or celebrities at Locarno? I wouldn’t describe it as the need for celebrities. The history of cinema is linked to the faces of the actors that we all love: John Wayne, Marlene Dietrich, James Stewart, Bette Davis, and Katharine Hepburn. We remember these people not because they are good-looking. They are, obviously, but we remember them because they were talented people. Someone like Katharine Hepburn could read a screenplay and say, “There are 20 pages too many.” Someone like Marcello Mastroianni, who always downplayed his being this super-talented artist, had a photographic memory and could learn everything by the first read. So, we need to make a difference between talents, stars and celebrities in the way we understand them now. Because someone like Marlene Dietrich is not just a star. She is also someone who could master how to address, for instance, the collective guilt of the German-speaking people during the war after the war, and keep the memory of it while still being the greatest star on Earth. So that’s a responsibility. And for me, actors are like the living history of cinema. People remember the great films through the stories of what happened to the character in that film. We know that High Noon is a highly political film made by a European director in Hollywood at the height of the witch hunt [of McCarthyism and the Hollywood blacklist], but we remember that film because it’s been incarnated in Gary Cooper’s body. Gary Cooper’s body was the messenger of American optimism, and now suddenly you have the very same American optimism that stands alone against a whole country, against a whole city, and he needs to fight for justice. How about some of the big names that Locarno will see this year or bold names with films in high-profile spots? The talents that we are privileged to feature on the Piazza Grande are all artists, such as Olivia Wilde [whose The Invite screens on the big outdoor square in Locarno this year]. When you read an interview with Olivia Wilde, you know that she’s a cinema person who knows what she’s talking about. Caleb Landry Jones is also famous because he played [Banshee] in the X-Men [franchise], and the got a Cannes award [for best actor in 2021 for his role in Justin Kurzel’s Nitram ], but he moves between different worlds of cinema. And then, for his new film, [the Locarno-premiering Down the Arm of God , directed by Peter Brunner], he put everything at stake to work with homeless people in Texas to tell us about the plight of these people who never sleep in the same place two nights in a row and what it means to be left behind. He spent some of his time as an artist living in the shoes of someone who might not even have shoes. Also, Claes Bang, [starring in the world-premiering I Is Another , directed by Felix Randau]. How debonair can a man be? I mean, it doesn’t get more debonair than him. But every film he picks is carefully picked. He could simply be playing the good-looking man and get away with it, and nobody would complain. But the choices he makes are always against his own persona, as if he’s always questioning things: “I invite you to look beyond the surface.” The film I Is Another is basically about this – a good-looking man who claims to have done something, but did he really do it? Claes Bang always digs deeper. So it’s very bold for him to take a role like that. Overall, the fact that we tend to think of these actors and people as just good-looking faces is a bit of an unfair assessment of what they do. Ultimately, we have so many nice faces, but only the talented ones stay. Since you just mentioned a specific film – not that I want to force you to choose between movies that you all clearly felt deserve a showcase – are there any films that you were particularly excited to get or that you didn’t even think would be in this year’s Locarno lineup? There are actually quite a few films. Among others, I’m very proud to have the Italian film Ketticè , produced by Luca Guadagnino, the second film by Giovanni Tortorici, who had his first film in Venice in Orizzonti (Horizons). Then I’m particularly glad to have A Margem Do Rio ( The Riverbank ) by Enock Carvalho and Matheus Farias, close collaborators of Kleber Mendonça Filho . I’m also very happy to have Violence du Corps de l’Autre ( Nobody’s Violence) by Denis Côté. He’s coming back to fiction film, quote unquote. I’m super happy to present to the international audience Wandering Trees ( Alberi Errante ) by Salvatore Mereu, a crucial Italian filmmaker who has the breadth of a 19th-century novelist. I would also point to the film Manhunt by Wayne Wapeemukwa. That’s a true-crime film,” but it comes from a specific place in Canadian culture. The director is a descendant of the First Nations, and the film questions the colonial myth of what is beyond the frontier and how this myth still affects people. There are also other films that I’m very proud of, such as Tear Gas by Uta Beria that documents the plight of the Georgian people of standing up against the Russian infiltration of their country, or Revolutionaries Never Die , a film about the legacy of the magnificent Lebanese filmmaker Jocelyne Saab. She is this extremely interesting filmmaker. I wouldn’t call her a documentarian because she was a filmmaker, and she chronicled the Lebanese civil war. She was on the ship Atlantis when [Yasser] Arafat had to leave Lebanon and landed in Tunis, Tunisia. She also documented with an uncanny eye for the future the onset of the Iranian revolution. She was this living memory of what was going on, and the film is basically about the work and the life of Jocelyne Saab as a living archive. And [Jean-Luc] Godard himself used some of her images. When you unveiled the program for Locarno 2026 , you spoke about how several films explore the theme of community… Yes, I think that stems from a sense of being threatened and being more vulnerable. I hope this doesn’t sound sanctimonious or corny, but we live in a moment where the future could be described as the Third World War in pieces. You have the war in Ukraine and in the region formerly called the Middle East – but middle of and from where is my question. Then you have Sudan, and then you have the economic takeovers of entire regions on the African continent. Plus, there is the erasure of civil rights, political rights, individual rights. So everything is coming together at the same time. What stays is this lingering and very uncomfortable fear that you are being threatened in the individuality of what your person is, if you are not a white Western person, and you can feel how things are shifting around you. People are being singled out for what they represent to each other, and what we represent to each other is not something that we decided. It’s something that has been put on us from above by a global block of linguistic conventions of what we are. This singling out of individuals is breaking up communities, and so people are really thinking about: How can we protect our communities? How can we come together again? But “together” not in a sense of let’s just be nice and cozy, cozy. Instead, let’s think differences, let’s think individualities, let’s think heritages, let’s think bodies, let’s think sexual orientation. And how can we bring all these things together? It’s not easy, but it’s exactly the thing that all these wars are threatening to suffocate. All these conversations that we need to have are being threatened. In a community, there is the opportunity, the possibility to speak, to talk, to make films, and to make a film is to engage with someone else to say: “What do you think about this?” Can we have a back-and-forth? So, communities today are the last vanguard of what it is to have and care about human dignity. Communities today are the laboratories where we can still think about how to make it all together. THR

If you haven’t seen any of his short- and medium-length movies yet, now may be the time. After all, his feature-length debut, September Afternoon , will world premiere on Aug. 10 in the Filmmakers of the Present Competition of the 79th edition of the Locarno Film Festival . It marks a return to Locarno for Schmidt, whose First Time [The Time for All but Sunset — Violet] got its world premiere at the Swiss festival in 2021, where it received a Pardi di Domani special mention. Related Stories TV Disney+ Greenlights 'House of Fates,' Spinoff of Hit Korean Fortune-Telling Series 'Battle of Fates' Lifestyle Paul Newman's Daughter Clea on the Charity He Built -- and Why She'll Never Retire From It Here is what we know about September Afternoon . “A couple refuses to accept that summer is over,” a synopsis tells us. “One last time, they head to the coast, to be together between sand dunes and sea water. But the blustery autumn wind is no substitute for the cozy rays of a summer sun. Desperate struggles against the encroaching elements become a brief interlude before the situation unravels into a disaster of a different magnitude. A contemporary cosmic catastrophe.” In his work, Schmidt lets images, sounds, music and moods do the talking, while spoken words are rarely necessary. The slow passage of time in everyday situations, repetition and silences are what interest the filmmaker. And it is what he presents to the viewer in ways that make you observe and wonder. His new cinematic experience, for example, turns romantic ideas of the summer on their head to paint a contemporary portrait of longing for connection steeped in resignation. Produced by Maxi Haslberger and Balthasar Busmann, September Afternoon features cinematography by Thomas Oswald. Schmidt, who was born in Leipzig in 1979 and lives and works in Hamburg as a filmmaker, video and conceptual artist, directed and edited the film based on his own screenplay. The cast is made up of Amin Motallebzadeh, Katharina Grossmann, Hedi Grossmann and Ada Kurzhöfer. Kino Rebelde is handling international sales. “The film uses ‘dead time’ as raw material,” Schmidt says about September Afternoon in a director’s note. “I stretch mundane moments until they collapse in their emptiness — an invitation to the viewer.” And he concludes: “In an age of arbitrary extraordinariness, plain banality is stimulating as fuck.” What can we add to that? It seems like this is the perfect time to simply mention that The Hollywood Reporter can premiere an exclusive clip from September Afternoon . Watch it right here. THR

title: Busan’s Asian Project Market Unveils 30 Selections for 2026 Edition

APM set a new all-time submissions record for the third consecutive year, receiving 604 entries from 48 countries. That marked an increase of 149 submissions year-on-year, following 455 submissions from 44 countries in 2025, 441 from 44 countries in 2024 and 399 from 50 countries in 2023. Submissions from Asia reached 423, up 82 from the previous year, while Korean submissions rose to 137, up 58. The lineup spans courtroom drama, coming-of-age story, family drama, crime thriller, queer romantic comedy, black comedy and mystery thriller, with the selected works touching on social realities, personal identity, family relationships and ethical tensions within communities. The slate mixes feature debuts from emerging filmmakers with new projects from directors already recognized on the festival circuit. Popular on Variety Three Japanese projects made the cut: “13” from Mori Tatsuya, who claimed BIFF’s New Currents prize in 2023 for “September 1923”; “Wings of Return (working title)” from Hirose Nanako; and “Yours” from Igarashi Kohei. Kyrgyzstan’s Dastan Zhapar Ryskeldi joins APM for a third time with “Bosogo,” while Sri Lanka’s Prasanna Vithanage presents “Islands,” following “Paradise,” which took the Jiseok prize at BIFF in 2023. India’s Dominic Sangma brings “Veil of Dust,” examining tragic contradictions within a community, and Tribeny Rai returns with her second project, “A Chronicle of Minor Things” (working title). Rounding out the region are Payal Sethi’s “Babak,” Stenzin Tankyong’s feature debut “Idiot (Kakthet)” and Pakistani director Eshah Shakeel’s feature debut “Dancers.” China, Hong Kong and Taiwan contributed four selections, pairing emerging filmmakers with experienced producers. Tibetan director Kangdrun presents “Orlo in the House,” Wang Zhiyi brings feature debut “Unripe,” Hong Kong’s So Chak Long enters with “Whisper of the Silence” and Taiwan’s Yen Hao-hsuan makes his first feature with “Uncle.” Southeast and West Asian entries include Aditya Ahmad’s feature directorial debut “Goldfish.” Ahmad previously took the top short-film prize in Venice’s Horizons sidebar in 2018. Reza Rahadian Matulessy follows debut feature “On Your Lap,” which picked up three prizes in BIFF’s Vision – Asia sidebar in 2025, with second feature “Casparina.” Cambodia’s Chheangkea has his first feature, “Little Phnom Penh,” selected, while the Philippines’ E Del Mundo brings “Once Upon a Time in the Philippines” and Iran’s Mehrnoush Alia presents “Bon Voyage.” Singapore’s Alvin Lee offers black comedy “Talk To Me When You Are Dead,” and Malaysia’s Tan Seng Kiat presents “One Fine Day,” which took the APM Next prize at TCCF 2025. Also selected are Thailand’s Panu Aree with “Fātimah” and Indonesia’s Mouly Surya with “The Wife Who Can See Dead People (Or Jinn).” Seven Korean projects round out the slate. Lee Sangcheol, whose films “Jesus Hospital,” “The Snob” and “Blesser” have all screened at BIFF, presents “PARK Deul-bi.” Choi Hyunyoung, whose “Memories of a Dead End” played in Korean Cinema Today – Panorama, brings “All’s Well That Ends Well,” and Lee Hanju, whose debut feature “The Waves of Winter” screened in the Korean Cinema Today – Vision strand, presents “The Family Table.” The remaining Korean selections are Park Syeyoung’s “Satellite of Love,” Park Joonho’s “Kuroshio” (Park also directed “3670”), actor-director Ryu Hyunkyung’s “Dog Fight” and novelist-filmmaker Kim Jinyeong’s “Red Hunger”; Kim previously directed “The Other Child.” The seven projects span psychological thriller, queer romantic comedy, black comedy, mystery thriller and drama. Selected projects will be nominated for awards backed by sponsors. ACFM is the official market of the Busan International Film Festival and is held in Busan every October. The 2025 edition, ACFM’s 20th, drew industry professionals from 55 countries – 3,024 of them, alongside 1,222 registered companies – with on-site attendance reaching a record 30,006. The Sales Market tallied 8,438 business meetings, generating an estimated $71.1 million in transactions. The 31st Busan International Film Festival runs Oct. 6-15, with the 21st ACFM held Oct. 10-13. title: ‘This Is Birmingham’: TV Series Adaptation Of Surprise Prime Video UK Hit In Works

The pic, made with a minimal budget, peaked at number five on Prime Video UK’s top ten films earlier this week, and creator Kay S. Ubhi told Deadline a TV series adaptation is now in development. The film, which Ubhi wrote and stars in, is billed as a “visceral crime drama” set in the depths of the UK’s brutal underworld. It follows AK (Ubhi), the inexperienced but ambitious son of a recently imprisoned Birmingham crime boss (Navdeep Monga), who steps up to lead the family business, only to be met by rival gangs determined to take over. The pic also stars the likes of Jerome Richards, Jag Patel and Wayne Nelson. Cowan, the UK film sales and production veteran, was among the producers of the indie pic and is also attached to the TV adaptation, Ubhi told Deadline in an interview today. We’re developing it with Bafta winner Michael L. Cowan, and the next step is bringing together the right production partners to take it into production.” Ubhi, who self-funded This is Birmingham , said his film had resonated with audiences, stacking up against Hollywood movies in the Prime Video charts, thanks to a “real audience for authentic British crime dramas” and was now being distributed in the U.S. on transactional on-demand platforms. He also pointed to the hot streak Birmingham, which is often referred to as England’s second city, has been on through the likes of Peaky Blinders and This Town . “The film offers a fresh unique perspective through its characters, emotional story and, of course, the Birmingham theme,” said Ubhi. “Birmingham already has a lot of intrigue because of its reputation and shows like Peaky Blinders .” As for funding the pic himself, “It was a huge personal commitment over several years, but I really believed in the story. title: Paramount Sacrificed Some Cinema History To Win Approval For Its Warner Deal, But Will It Be Enough To Safeguard Europe’s Theatrical Business?
full_text: Skip to main content By Jake Kanter Jake Kanter International Investigations Editor @Jake_Kanter More Stories By Jake Paramount Sacrificed Some Cinema History To Win Approval For Its Warner Deal, But Will It Be Enough To Safeguard Europe’s Theatrical Business? Jared Leto Denies Criminal Sexual Conduct: “I Have Never Sexually Assaulted Anyone” ‘Blankety Blank,’ ‘Celebrity Mastermind’ & ‘Live At The Apollo’ All Canceled By The BBC Under Sweeping Content Cuts View All July 30, 2026 12:00am Paramount CEO David Ellison Getty “Cinema may have peaked,” was how United International Pictures sales manager Kenneth Jønsson greeted the arrival of The Odyssey in Norway. “Trust me, this is one for the ages, and a huge reminder of how lucky we are to work with films and filmmakers like this.” Jønsson posted his love letter to Christopher Nolan’s epic on LinkedIn just before the movie’s premiere. A couple of weeks on, there are very real questions about the future of United International Pictures (UIP) and whether it will continue to serve the filmmakers Jønsson admires. That’s because Paramount has agreed to exit UIP, its 50-50 joint venture with Universal Pictures , to secure regulatory approval for its takeover of Warner Bros. Discovery in the European Union. In remedies laid down by the European Commission, the EU’s antitrust enforcer, Paramount will need to unwind its links to UIP within 13 months of closing the Warner merger, walking away from a company that has been part of the European cinema landscape for 44 years. Watch on Deadline Related Stories Culture Joyce Carol Oates Defends Christopher Nolan & 'The Odyssey' Against Emily Wilson, Other Critics Books 'The Final Girl Support Group' Heads To Paramount As Film Directed & Adapted By Christopher Landon; Aperture & Muschiettis' Double Dream Producing Paramount declined to comment on how it will disentangle itself from UIP or whether the venture will continue without its stewardship. Universal Pictures also declined to comment on the European Commission ruling last week. UIP did not respond to a request for comment. UIP distributed ‘The Odyssey’ Melinda Sue Gordon/Universal So here’s what we know: Paramount will terminate its 50% stake in UIP, meaning it will have to seek alternative distribution arrangements in the 100 territories in which UIP has a presence. Paramount may be able to tap into Warner Bros. Pictures operations in some of these locations or piggyback on Warner’s existing partnerships, but only if the partner has no role in distributing Universal or Disney films. When Warner had a distribution deal with SF Studios in the Nordics, for example, if Paramount had wanted to switch its UIP films into this agreement, it would have needed to establish that SF Studios had no similar arrangements with Universal and Disney. This would ensure Paramount does not fall foul of European Commission conditions. Whatever the outcome, UIP will have significantly fewer titles to handle, which will inevitably create uncertainty for the company’s 200 employees (even if it does distribute some non-Paramount-Universal titles, such as Lionsgate’s Michael ). Headquartered in Chiswick, a leafy suburb of west London, UIP does not have a CEO, though former STX Entertainment executive Rhiannon Harries serves as chief operating officer and appears to be one of the company’s most senior figures. Paramount and Universal lawyers act as directors of UIP’s British operations. UIP posted sales of nearly £198M ($263M) in 2024, per its most recent accounts filed at the UK’s Companies House. It recorded a pre-tax profit of £12.2M. In its pomp, UIP boasted box office takings of $2.5 billion, but was much diminished in 2007, when Paramount and Universal took direct control of distribution in key markets, including France, Brazil, and Italy. Stewart Till, the British executive who ran UIP for four years until 2006, said Paramount’s exit would be the end of an era for a company that combined the “best of Hollywood with local decision makers.” He said the exit was “not irrelevant” for Paramount given that it will have to make alternative arrangements in UIP territories. “It’s not a coincidence that Paramount hasn’t done that since 2007,” he said. There is a feeling, however, that divesting from UIP is a small concession for Paramount to make in the context of an industry-reshaping $111B union with Warner Bros. A well-placed industry executive said: “I can’t see it making any difference, to be honest. The pieces will just move around between even fewer players, meaning even less competition. Maybe there needs to be further regulation introduced so that no single local distribution company has dominant market share, and other ways to stimulate competition and innovation.” The International Union of Cinemas (UNIC), which represents cinema operators across 39 European territories, agrees. Laura Houlgatte, UNIC’s chief executive, told Deadline: “While the remedy addresses an important structural issue, it does not tackle similar risks that arise from theatrical distribution arrangements outside the UIP territories, nor does the Commission decision address a number of wider concerns that UNIC raised throughout the review.” UIP re-released ‘Top Gun’ and ‘Top Gun: Maverick’ in cinemas earlier this year Paramount During the European Commission’s investigation process, Houlgatte said the UNIC advocated for “safeguards around theatrical exclusivity and release windows, as well as measures to help maintain a strong and diverse pipeline of films for cinemas and audiences.” Paramount CEO David Ellison has attempted to assuage these concerns with commitments to release more than 30 cinema films a year and hold to a minimum theatrical window of 45 days. He will continue making this case while the merger is on ice as Paramount fights a lawsuit from 12 U.S. state attorneys general, who argue the deal stifles competition for theatrical film distribution. The Balanced Economy Project, an apolitical UK non-profit that lobbies against monopolies, is not convinced. It said the European Commission’s UIP remedy “does nothing obvious about the future bargaining power of a combined Paramount-Warner studio.” The Balanced Economy Project added: “Cinemas would still face one fewer independent major studio. Broadcasters and platforms would still face a larger owner of premium rights. Producers and creative suppliers would still face another reduction in major routes to market.” Paramount breaking bonds with Universal signals the end of some European cinema history, but discovering whether it’s enough to safeguard a precarious business from a new monolith will be its own odyssey of sorts.
