title: ‘The Bombing of Pan Am 103’ Review: Netflix’s Sensitive Lockerbie Drama Is Restrained to a Fault
full_text: × Skip to main content By Angie Han Plus Icon Angie Han Television Critic ajhan Follow Sign Up View All July 30, 2026 12:00am Connor Swindells in 'The Bombing of Pan Am 103.' Courtesy of Netflix “If the word Lockerbie will be associated with this terrible tragedy,” intones a priest at a memorial ceremony, “perhaps it will also be spoken of in the future with admiration through the example of its people.” And so it is in The Bombing of Pan Am 103 , Netflix’s new chronicle of the 1988 attack that claimed 270 lives. It is the people of this small Scottish town, Jonathan Lee’s drama makes clear, who rushed to one another’s aid in the crisis, who worked tirelessly to pursue answers, who embraced mourners from around the world. As a tribute to their compassion and tenacity in the face of horror, the six-part miniseries is above reproach — respectful and respectable, laudatory but dignified. Related Stories Lifestyle Odessa A'Zion and Connor Swindells Honored by Chopard in Cannes: "Really Weird, Crazy and Surreal" Lifestyle Chopard Gala to Host Godmother Isabelle Huppert and Honorees Odessa A'zion and Connor Swindells The Bombing of Pan Am 103 The Bottom Line Respectable but not memorable. Airdate: Thursday, July 30 (Netflix) Cast: Connor Swindells, Patrick J. Adams, Merritt Wever, Peter Mullan, Eddie Marsan, Tony Curran, Phyllis Logan, James Harkness, Nicholas Gleaves, Molly Geddes Creator: Jonathan Lee As a story trying to stand its own test of time, however, the series leaves something to be desired. Better equipped to pore over the past than reflect on its enduring significance, The Bombing of Pan Am 103 , starring Connor Swindells and Patrick J. Adams , delivers a less-than-memorable portrait of an indelible event. To recap, for those who do not recall the original events (or, for that matter, the 2025 series Lockerbie: A Search for Truth ): On the night of Dec. 21, a commercial plane en route from London to New York exploded about 60 miles outside Glasgow, killing everyone on board plus several more on the ground. If what exactly had transpired was not immediately obvious — it takes the better part of the Michael Keillor-directed premiere for law enforcement and intelligence agencies to determine it was a bombing at all, and then four of the next five hours to figure out who was behind it — the magnitude of the destruction is. The physical debris was scattered over a massive area of roughly 800 square miles. The emotional and political wreckage was spread further still, with victims from 21 countries (including 179 from the U.S., spurring the involvement of the FBI), hundreds of bereaved and countless witnesses, detectives, lawyers and more involved in the aftermath. With a scope so unwieldy, Lee does what he can to keep his drama efficient, sensitive, human-scaled. From that vast population of people directly affected by the incident, he trains his attention on a few key figures, including a dogged Scottish police officer, Ed McCusker (Swindells), and a slippery FBI agent, Dick Marquise (Adams). In relaying the unimaginable destruction of the event, Lee eschews sensationalism for sobriety. Graphic violence or gore are nowhere to be seen, and even the crash itself is depicted through the horror of Lockerbie residents stumbling outside to find their world transformed into rubble and hellfire, rather than through the terror experienced by those on the plane. At its best, this restraint dovetails with the story unfolding before us. The Scottish and American teams piece together their theory painstakingly over time, poring over clues as small as a torn clothing label and negotiating every single disclosure with their counterparts across borders. Similarly, Lee assembles his story via small but striking details: the eerie orange of a burning sky at night, the blood-red smattering of pins on an evidence board, a child’s shoe lost in the grass. But the necessity of paring down such a massive event has the effect of flattening the very elements that ought to give it its texture and heft — namely, the people involved. McCusker and Marquise, the closest thing this shifting and sprawling ensemble has to main characters, are allowed barely any room to be individuals with their own motives or personalities. Instead, they’re made to symbolize everything valiant and determined about the Scottish investigators and everything well-meaning but misguided about their American colleagues, respectively. A few of the supporting players stand out despite the vague archetypes they’re given to play — notably Peter Mullan as a wonderfully gruff police superintendent, Merritt Wever as a relentless advocate for the victims and, less favorably, Eddie Marsan affecting a bizarre Southern accent as an FBI bomb expert. But for the most part, the further the narrative strays from the search at its center, the clunkier its reliance on synecdoche becomes. An otherwise forgettable cop (James Harkness) is described as having a good memory, so that he can later bemoan this quality, so that he can stand in for every first responder traumatized by recollections of that night. A local (Phyllis Logan) spearheading the effort to return victims’ effects to their families spouts clichés like, “We just saw something that needed to be done, so we did it,” so that we can understand the entire population of Lockerbie to be generous and resolute by extension. Meanwhile, as dogged as the characters are in pursuing questions of who and how, the show is rather less interested in reflecting on what any of it means in a bigger-picture sense. We’re told the incident led to sweeping reforms in the airline industry, but not what those changes actually were. We’re informed the global implications of this crime are huge, but given no sense of what changed internationally as a result. The very existence of this show would seem to prove the bombing left a lasting impression on the Scottish psyche, but the precise contours of that impression go unexplored. If the logic is that those who lived through those days won’t need any explanation, the flaw is that four decades on, the ratio of people who clearly remember Lockerbie to those who don’t is only shrinking. Or perhaps the show’s lack of bigger answers is simply an acknowledgment that there are none, really, to be found. No amount of historical context can soothe a devastated parent’s pain. No geopolitical analysis can justify a community’s heartbreak. No outcome can bring back the lives that were ended. In that light, the bare fact that hundreds of people were murdered that day, and that hundreds more stepped up to comfort their loved ones, to bring the perpetrators to justice, to agitate for change, is worth trying to remember in itself, however imperfectly. If The Bombing of Pan Am 103 struggles to find the specific humanity of its generic characters, the impulse behind creating them in the first place — to commemorate those departed, and those who cared about them — cannot help but feel touchingly humane. THR

title: Thanh Hang, Hong Anh’s Vietnamese Period Drama ‘Madame in Saigon’ Lands North American Rights Deal With Reel Citrus, Live On (EXCLUSIVE)
full_text: Jul 29, 2026 11:55pm PT Thanh Hang, Hong Anh’s Vietnamese Period Drama ‘Madame in Saigon’ Lands North American Rights Deal With Reel Citrus, Live On (EXCLUSIVE) By Naman Ramachandran Plus Icon Naman Ramachandran Latest ‘Ramayana’ Trailer: Ranbir Kapoor and Yash Face Off in First Part of Nitesh Tiwari’s Epic 1 hour ago Busan’s Asian Project Market Unveils 30 Selections for 2026 Edition 4 hours ago Thanh Hang, Hong Anh’s Vietnamese Period Drama ‘Madame in Saigon’ Lands North American Rights Deal With Reel Citrus, Live On (EXCLUSIVE) 4 hours ago See All Reel Citrus/Live On Reel Citrus has acquired North American rights to the Vietnamese period drama “Mesdames Thanh Sắc,” which it will release as “ Madame in Saigon ,” through a partnership with Ho Chi Minh City-based production and rights partner Live On. Directed by Thắng Vũ, “Madame in Saigon” is set in 1960s Saigon and follows dancer Cầm Thanh (Thanh Hằng) as she rises through the city’s nightlife into a power struggle with Madame Sắc (Hồng Ánh), owner of the Kim Đô nightclub. The cast also includes Lương Thế Thành and singer-actor Văn Mai Hương. The film opened in Vietnam in June. Related Stories Christopher Nolan's Oscar 'Odyssey': Can Matt Damon, Monsters and Mythology Deliver Another Best Picture Statue? BAFTA Tweaks Film Awards Rules, Expands Outstanding British Film Longlist and Updates AI Guidance Reel Citrus will hold a red-carpet premiere in Los Angeles on Aug. 26, with Thanh Hằng in attendance. The actor rose to fame as Vietnam’s preeminent supermodel in the 2010s before moving into dramatic film roles, with credits including “Mẹ chồng” (“Mother-in-Law”) and “Những cô gái chân dài.” She has also served as a longtime judge on “Vietnam’s Next Top Model.” Popular on Variety Following the premiere, Thanh Hằng will join a press junket in Orange County alongside local community organizations. The wider campaign will extend across digital platforms and include creator support, as well as Vietnamese Student Associations across the U.S. and Canada. “‘Madame in Saigon’ is exactly the kind of story we built Reel Citrus to champion, bold, unapologetically Vietnamese, and made to travel,” said Brittany Tran, executive director of Reel Citrus. “Our job is to build the audience around the film to make sure our communities see themselves on screen and show up for each other. Partnering with Live On to bring this film and Thanh Hằng to North American audiences is a milestone for us, and just the beginning,” Tran added. Founded in 2025, Reel Citrus has previously led theatrical marketing campaigns for “Leaving Mom” and “Ancestral Home.” Its next release, “Summer School, 2001,” is slated for October. The deal marks Live On’s first U.S. collaboration and its debut in the North American theatrical market. The Ho Chi Minh City studio has spent more than a decade producing multi-genre Vietnamese films. The film opens across North America on Aug. 28. Jamie McCarthy/Getty Images; Brenda Chase/Online USA, Inc. Logo text It was “really funny” for Homer Gere and Kaia Gerber to be working together on The Shards following their parents’ romantic history. While chatting with E! News at the New York City premiere of Ryan Murphy ‘s new FX series, both actors opened up about their experience sharing the screen 30 years after Cindy Crawford and Richard Gere divorced in 1995. Crawford later remarried Rande Gerber in 1998 and they welcomed Kaia in 2001, while Richard Gere and Carey Lowell got married in 2002, two years after Homer was born. The latter couple ultimately divorced in 2016 and Richard has since tied the knot again with Alejandra Silva. From the inside, it’s really normal.” “We just became friends as coworkers before we started working, and she’s become a really close friend. It’s been lovely working with her,” the Euphoria actor continued. Kaia echoed a similar sentiment on the red carpet, saying she had “never met Homer until we started filming,” despite both their parents still working in the entertainment industry throughout the last three decades. “It was so lovely to work with him,” the Palm Royale actress added. “He’s so wonderful. He’s so funny. He makes me laugh so hard and he’s the greatest scene partner ever. And really it’s just such a supportive environment and we’ve gotten so close over this process.” The Shards , adapted from Bret Easton Ellis’ book of the same name, follows a group of privileged high school friends as a serial killer strikes across Los Angeles in 1981. Elsewhere on the red carpet, Kaia spoke with The Hollywood Reporter about her reaction to when she first learned Murphy would be adapting Ellis’ novel for the small screen. “I’m a huge Bret Easton Ellis fan and when this book came out, I read it immediately and read it over and over again,” she said. “Then when I heard Ryan was doing it, I’m also the biggest fan of Ryan. He gave me my first ever job. When he told me he got the rights to it , I just got chills and teared up.” The series premieres Aug. 5 on FX. THR

title: ‘Spider-Man: Brand New Day’ Aims to Make Box Office History as It Targets High-Flying Opening
full_text: × Skip to main content By Ryan Gajewski Plus Icon Ryan Gajewski Senior Entertainment Reporter View All July 29, 2026 7:29pm MJ (Zendaya) watches Spider-Man work in 'Spider-Man: Brand New Day.' Jay Maidment/Sony Pictures Logo text Spider-Man : Brand New Day looks to close out the month with a big swing, as Sony Pictures ‘ latest superhero feature with Tom Holland and Zendaya eyes an astronomical opening weekend at the box office . After Universal’s The Odyssey enjoyed quite the successful box office journey without major new competition for the past two weeks, Peter Parker and his pals are poised to land the year’s biggest debut and potentially one of the top-grossing openings ever. The studio is projecting a domestic opening of $195 million from 4,300 North American theaters, which is also in line with third-party tracking services. Related Stories Movies Joyce Carol Oates Defends 'Odyssey' Against Translator's Viral Slam: "Crude Language of MAGA Folks" Movies 'Spider-Man: Brand New Day' Swings to China's Biggest Superhero Opening in Seven Years This would top last month’s launch for Disney ‘s Toy Story 5 , which opened to $159.6 million domestically, to make Spider-Man: Brand New Day the biggest debut of 2026. This would also put it in the top 10 for domestic opening weekends, beating 2019’s photorealistic The Lion King remake, which holds the No. 10 launch at $191.7 million. The last time a title opened above $200 million domestically was two years ago with Deadpool & Wolverine at $211.4 million. (The record goes to Avengers: Endgame’ s wild 2019 opening of $357.1 million.) Sony projects Spider-Man: Brand New Day to add $270 million from international markets for a global start of $465 million, including a strong showing in China . This would give it the studio’s second-best launch behind Spider-Man: No Way Home ‘ s heroic opening of $600.5 million in 2021, and it would best Spider-Man 3′ s $381.6 million start from 2007. Spider-Man and The Punisher ( Jon Bernthal ) in Spider-Man: Brand New Day. Jay Maidment/Sony Pictures Exhibitors are certainly clamoring to show director Destin Daniel Cretton ‘s new Spider-Man film, which centers on the title hero living a lonely existence without his loved ones before a dangerous new foe targets him. Hailing from Sony and Marvel Studios , Brand New Day accounts for 49 percent of this weekend’s showtimes as of Wednesday, according to the Boxoffice Company, as opposed to the 22 percent that The Odyssey held when it opened two weekends ago to $124.5 million domestically for the third-biggest 2026 launch to date. Word of mouth could push the Brand New Day opening much higher, as the film is already off to a flying start with critics. Also starring Sadie Sink , Jacob Batalon , Jon Bernthal and Mark Ruffalo , it holds a 91 percent approval rating from reviewers on Rotten Tomatoes. That puts it within similar range of the franchise’s other recent offerings, including 2018’s animated Spider-Man: Into the Spider-Verse at 97 percent and Spider-Man: No Way Home at 93 percent. In his review for The Hollywood Reporter , chief film critic David Rooney writes that Brand New Da y “foregrounds the humanity that has always been Spidey’s greatest strength,” and he praises “a never-better Tom Holland.” Indeed, some analysts are predicting that the buzz around the release will carry Spider-Man: Brand New Day far beyond $195 million. It remains to be seen whether the $260.1 million domestic opening sum for No Way Home , the previous live-action Spider-Man release, could potentially be within reach. Granted, that one had the benefit of the buzz surrounding the return of past Peter Parkers in Tobey Maguire and Andrew Garfield, not to mention that the release faced no real competition and marked the first post-COVID theatrical visit for many moviegoers who were starved for entertainment experiences. Notably, there has been recent debate about audiences tiring of franchise offerings, given the underperformance of titles from both the superhero variety ( June’s Supergirl ) and otherwise ( May’s The Mandalorian and Grogu ). And yet, this weekend is poised to prove that the filmmaking teams have done an admirable job of handling Marvel Comics’ crown-jewel hero. As Fandango director of analytics and Box Office Theory founder Shawn Robbins tells THR , “Tom Holland, Sony and Marvel Studios’ run of films has remained remarkably fresh, thanks to thoughtful timing and stories that continue to connect with audiences in both new and familiar ways.” He adds, “They’ve consistently met — and often exceeded — expectations, anchored by the kind of character-driven storytelling and big-screen spectacle audiences want from Spider-Man. It’s as much a gold standard as any for how to keep a massively popular character relevant and endearing to multiple generations of moviegoers.” As for Holland, whose first leading role as the character came with 2017’s Spider-Man: Homecoming , it appears likely that Sony will have more chances to continue its winning streak. “It has been the gift of my life,” the actor — who also appears in The Odyssey — told THR at the Brand New Day premiere in Los Angeles about playing Spidey. “I will do it for as long as they’ll have me. So if this movie does good, I guess we’ll see!” Yes, we will. THR

title: Grammys CEO “Saddened” Over BTS Decision to Not Submit for Awards
full_text: × Skip to main content By Ethan Millman Plus Icon Ethan Millman Music Editor View All July 29, 2026 6:12pm Jungkook, V, Jin, RM, Suga, Jimin and J-Hope of BTS speak onstage during the 52nd American Music Awards at MGM Grand Garden Arena on May 25, 2026, in Las Vegas, Nevada. Ethan Miller/Getty Images Recording Academy CEO Harvey Mason Jr. has issued a lengthy response after BTS announced they wouldn’t be submitting their music for Grammy consideration this year, giving his support to the group over their decision while also addressing critique toward the organization’s newly-created best Asian pop music performance category. “I am saddened to hear that BTS has chosen not to participate in the Grammy Awards process this year, but as a music creator, I understand and respect their decision,” Mason Jr. wrote. “I do want to clarify something that seems to be getting lost in the conversation. The Asian Pop category was created to celebrate the depth, diversity and extraordinary growth of pop artistry coming out of Asia. The spirit of this new category is to shine a dedicated spotlight on these important artists.” Related Stories Music White House Claps Back at Noah Kahan for Criticizing Trump's Use of His Song Music BTS Will Not Be Submitting to 2027 Grammy Awards BTS first announced their decision on Tuesday night, sharing posts on Instagram where they said they “hope that music can be heard and loved for what it is, rather than being divided by region or language.” The move came just over a month after the Recording Academy first introduced its new Asian pop category, which, per the Academy, “recognizes artistic excellence in Asian pop music performances originating from or widely recognized within Asian markets, including but not limited to K-pop, J-pop and C-pop, with meaningful use of one or more Asian languages. Awards are presented to the performing artist(s).” The award had received a mixed response from fans, with some arguing the award could keep Asian acts from getting properly recognized in the general categories. In his statement, Mason Jr. said the genre categories don’t”exclude an artist from also submitting and being considered in the General Field.” “Recognition in a genre category and recognition in the General Field are not mutually exclusive,” Mason Jr. said. “An artist can absolutely pursue both.” Mason Jr. further wrote that the Academy adds new categories “never to divide, but to expand who is recognized by our 15,000 Grammy voters.” “The Grammy organization is here to serve music and all the people who make it,” Mason Jr. wrote. “As we continue to expand the reach, our membership and our awards, regardless of geography or language, I want to emphasize that we will continue to listen to the global music community and work to honor and celebrate all the artists whose music moves the world.” BTS isn’t the first act to rebuke the Grammys, as other major stars including The Weeknd, Drake and Morgan Wallen have all decided in recent years not to have their music considered as well. Read Mason Jr.’s full statement below: I am saddened to hear that BTS has chosen not to participate in the Grammy Awards process this year, but as a music creator, I understand and respect their decision. I do want to clarify something that seems to be getting lost in the conversation. The Asian Pop category was created to celebrate the depth, diversity and extraordinary growth of pop artistry coming out of Asia. The spirit of this new category is to shine a dedicated spotlight on these important artists. More categories mean more artists’ work is recognized. It’s never to divide, but to expand who is recognized by our 15,000 Grammy voters. I also want to be very clear: submitting music in a genre category such as Asian Pop, or Jazz or Country does not exclude an artist from also submitting and being considered in the General Field categories, including Record of the Year, Album of the Year and Song of the Year. Those categories remain open to any eligible recording, regardless of genre. Recognition in a genre category and recognition in the General Field are not mutually exclusive. An artist can absolutely pursue both. The Grammy organization is here to serve music and all the people who make it. As we continue to expand the reach, our membership and our awards, regardless of geography or language, I want to emphasize that we will continue to listen to the global music community and work to honor and celebrate all the artists whose music moves the world.” THR

title: Deadline revealed last week
full_text: Skip to main content By Jake Kanter Jake Kanter International Investigations Editor @Jake_Kanter More Stories By Jake Talent Agent Mark Jermin Strongly Refuted Unlawful Activity. A Leaked Contract Raises Questions About His Denial. Paramount Sacrificed Some Cinema History To Win Approval For Its Warner Deal, But Will It Be Enough To Safeguard Europe’s Theatrical Business? Jared Leto Denies Criminal Sexual Conduct: “I Have Never Sexually Assaulted Anyone” View All July 23, 2026 5:09am Mark Jermin Gareth Danks EXCLUSIVE : A prominent British children’s acting agency, which has helped young performers clinch roles in Harry Potter and Hunger Games, could have broken UK agency law by effectively charging actors training fees for the opportunity to secure representation, according to legal experts. In emails seen by Deadline, Mark Jermin Management (MJM) encouraged multiple young people to attend paid-for acting classes, provided by sister company the Mark Jermin Stage School (MJSS), if they wished to be represented by the agency. UK law prohibits entertainment agencies from charging upfront fees for representing their clients. Agencies are only permitted to make money by charging a commission on the fees their clients earn from acting work. Agency law experts said Deadline’s findings raised questions about whether MJM breached these regulations. Related Stories Casting 'Harry Potter' Series Star Ruari Spooner Joins Bill Burr & Chris O'Dowd In Comedy 'Bender' News Lady Gaga Scores Emmy Nomination For "The Dead Dance" From Netflix's 'Wednesday' A spokesperson for MJM founder Mark Jermin strongly denied that representation has “ever been contingent upon the purchase of training services.” Jermin declined to comment on specific examples, with his lawyer stating that it was “impossible” for him to address the allegations because Deadline had refused to hand over copies of the original emails. Deadline did not disclose the original messages for source protection reasons. Watch on Deadline The allegations follow Jermin’s earlier acknowledgment that his company mishandled self-tape auditions, prompted by a Deadline investigation in May . After publication, Jermin described the piece as “deeply unfair,” in part because he said the allegations of audition malpractice were historical and isolated. Since that investigation, Deadline has obtained further evidence of at least two other instances of self-tape audition issues. This includes an incident in January, when a disabled actor felt misled by MJM after being asked to record a self-tape audition and post about it on social media, even though he had not been called to audition by the casting team. Through his attorney, Jermin admitted to mistakes in his company’s dealings with the disabled actor. “We recognise that further concerns and allegations have been raised following recent reporting and we take them extremely seriously,” Jermin’s spokesperson added. “However, we deny unequivocally allegations of deliberate wrongdoing, unlawful conduct or systemic misconduct.” Jermin has engaged an external consultant to review processes at MJM and MJSS with a view to making improvements. Jermin’s lawyer declined to identify the consultancy or its terms of reference. Acting Lessons Linked To Representation Jermin is one of the UK’s best-known children’s agents, unearthing talent including Heartstopper star Kit Connor and Wednesday ’s Evie Templeton, as well as securing roles for actors like Eire Farrell in the Harry Potter series. He has parlayed his expertise into a significant social media presence, which he uses to promote his management work and market acting lessons, promising to make stars out of young people. Jermin’s TikTok updates are a legitimate way to sell services and discover new talent, but behind his popular videos, he has used tactics that have raised questions. Kit Connor in ‘Heartstopper’ Samuel Dore/Netflix/Courtesy Everett Collection Deadline has obtained emails and messages spanning a four-year period from January 2021 to October 2025 in which MJM employees, including Jermin himself, told individuals enquiring about representation that the agency prefers to take on new talent through acting classes. UK law generally prohibits agencies like MJM from charging upfront fees and prevents them from making the provision of representation conditional upon the use of other services, such as acting classes. The messages show that MJM repeatedly told students and parents that it “scouts” new clients from lessons. On other occasions, the company was more direct. In one 2023 email, an MJM representative told a parent that the company “only represents” young actors “who regularly train and attend our classes.” Separately, in a 2022 WhatsApp message, Jermin stated that actors “need” to attend a course to be considered for MJM’s new voice work division. Deadline has also received testimony from a dozen current and former Mark Jermin Stage School students/parents, who said it was their understanding that they needed to pay for lessons to be considered for representation. “If you weren’t in the classes, there was no chance you would be signed,” one person alleged. Deadline presented the evidence to three lawyers and two industry experts, all of whom have an understanding of the relevant UK agency law. They said the messages were grounds to suspect that MJM could be in breach of Regulation 5 of the Conduct of Employment Agencies and Employment Businesses Regulations 2003, which states that agencies must not make work-finding services conditional upon work-seekers using other services. The regulations are enforced by the Fair Work Agency, which has the power to inspect agencies. If an agent is found to have flouted the law, they could be fined if they do not put their house in order, though this is rare. The Fair Work Agency declined to comment on MJM, but said it would examine any relevant complaints. “Open & Shut” Case Paul Maynard, a partner in employment law at Gaby Hardwicke Solicitors, said: “On the evidence I have seen, and from Regulation 5, this agency is in breach of the regulations. It seems pretty open and shut, and I can’t see any exemption within the regulations.” In one 2023 message to a parent, MJM explained that having children in classes promotes high standards and allows MJM and MJSS employees to get to know young people before they are put forward for casting opportunities. MJM added that attending lessons is not an “automatic” route to representation as the agency “can’t take on every student.” Similar language is contained in MJSS’s terms and conditions, which state: “Participation in training does not guarantee representation.” Maynard explained: “Regarding language around ‘scouting’ or ‘vetting’ in classes, there’s no wriggle room in Regulation 5 that allows them [MJM] to do it. They’re charging for those classes, and that’s an ancillary service to what they then go and do, which is supply clients for hire and reward.” Seth Roe, a partner at Wiggin, which recently represented casting directory Spotlight in a High Court triumph against Equity in a case relating to agency laws, said: “An agency should not say (or imply) that it will only help a person find work if they also buy an extra service from the agency or from someone connected with the agency. “The reason for the rule is straightforward: access to work should not be used as leverage to pressure actors, performers, models or other work seekers into paying for add-ons they may not need, may not be able to afford, or may feel they have no real choice but to purchase.” He added that a court would likely take a literal interpretation of the regulations, which is to protect work seekers from being exploited. “That could therefore lead to a broad, practical and purposive interpretation, focused on whether a work seeker (or their parents, guardians etc) could reasonably have felt pressured to pay for additional services in order to have a better prospect of securing work,” Roe said. Dugald Johnson, agents’ official at actors’ union Equity, told Deadline: “The law is clear that the only fee an agency may charge a performer is a fee out of earnings from work — commission. Agencies should understand that they cannot make representation conditional upon paying upfront fees, whether for acting classes or any other service. “If members are asked for such fees, Equity advises them not to pay them and to contact the union. It is incumbent on all agencies to engage with and observe basic rules which apply to them, including on fees, not least given the immense trust which performers place in them.” Adrian Marlowe, a Lawspeed attorney who contributed to government thinking when the laws were drafted, said Regulation 5 was engaged because MJM and MJSS are connected and the latter is charging a fee. He added that, although MJM’s emails are not explicitly transactional, they “do indicate that this could be a breach of Regulation 5.” Another industry professional, who has experience in agency laws but did not wish to be named in connection with Jermin, said: “An agency should not require a prospective client to purchase classes, coaching, workshops, photography, or other services as a condition of being considered for representation or for access to employment opportunities.” In a statement, Jermin’s spokesperson said that MJM denies “unequivocally allegations of deliberate wrongdoing, unlawful conduct or systemic misconduct. In particular, we strongly reject any suggestion that representation by Mark Jermin Management has ever been contingent upon the purchase of training services.” Jermin declined to engage with the specific examples presented by Deadline. His lawyer said that it was “impossible” for his client to address the allegations because Deadline had declined to hand over unedited copies of the original emails for source protection reasons. The attorney claimed that a document prepared by Deadline detailing the messages had been edited “significantly,” including quoting extracts “entirely out of context.” Deadline does not accept that any messages were edited to change their meaning. Jermin has also previously “emphatically denied” any unlawful charging. “MJM does not charge, and has never charged, any individual to be managed or represented by it,” his lawyer said in a letter to Deadline in March, adding: “Never has it ever been put to students participating in stage school classes operated by TMJSS that they may be represented by MJM at some point in the future provided that they continue paying to participate in those stage classes.” Self-Tape Mishandling After Deadline published its original investigation into self-tape auditions by Jermin and his companies in May, he posted a statement saying that the allegations regarding the mishandling of self-tapes in 2024 were “historical,” while in correspondence to Deadline through a lawyer, he blamed the issues on administrative staff at his stage school. Deadline has now seen evidence that raises questions about his defense, implicating Jermin in the alleged mishandling of auditions as recently as January. Jermin’s position is that these were isolated mistakes, shorn of context, and were not indicative of “persistent misconduct.” Theatre Royal Bath At the start of 2026, MJM sent an actor an audition for a production of The Secret Garden at The Egg, which is part of the Theatre Royal Bath. Casey, a pseudonym we are using to protect the disabled actor’s identity, believed it to be a legitimate audition. Days earlier, Jermin had told Casey he was pitching him for the role, so when the actor received the audition, he assumed the pitch was successful. Jermin requested that Casey post a social media video thanking MJM for securing him the audition. Casey followed instructions, ending his video by stating: “Thanks so much to the team at Mark Jermin Management for helping to secure me this audition.” After reading Deadline’s story in May, Casey became suspicious about The Secret Garden self-tape and contacted the Theatre Royal Bath. The theater said Casey had not been called to audition and that the casting team had not received his self-tape from MJM. “To find out that something that I put so much effort into was a fabrication was heartbreaking,” Casey told Deadline. He feels misled and exploited, believing he was encouraged to deceive his social media followers. Through his lawyer, Jermin said Casey’s experience was the result of miscommunication at MJM. After talking to Casey about pitching him for the role, Jermin believed a colleague had submitted his audition to the Theatre Royal Bath when, in reality, they had only sent Casey’s acting resume. Jermin’s attorney described it as an “unfortunate error” that he “very much regrets,” but said it was not evidence of “persistent and long-standing wrongdoing regarding the handling of self-tape auditions.” Casey challenged Jermin directly about the self-tape issue over email in May, during which the MJM founder said he had “proof” that the tape was sent. Through his lawyer, he later admitted that this evidence did not exist. Jermin accepted that he should have been more careful in his communication with Casey. Jermin attempted to talk to Casey to explain, but the actor declined. Jermin’s correspondence with the Theatre Royal Bath team also contained misinformation about Casey. He claimed that Casey “sometimes” presents Blue Peter , the iconic BBC kids’ show. Casey has never hosted Blue Peter . Jermin’s spokesperson said: “We understand that some individuals may have had experiences that they were unhappy with and, where mistakes have occurred, we regret any distress caused and remain committed to reviewing and improving our processes. To this end, we have retained the services of an independent consultant who will be reviewing all our processes.” In a second example from January 2023, Jermin emailed an actor we are anonymizing as Max, requesting that he self-tape for a Rice Krispies advert. Jermin copied and pasted a message purporting to be from the casting director. The message contained Max’s full name, suggesting that he was unambiguously the recipient of the audition. When Max requested further information about the role directly from the casting team, he was told that Jermin likely sent the self-tape in “error,” because he had not been called to audition. Jermin’s attorney said his client did not know the identity of Max and was unable to find any record of the audition for the Rice Krispies advert. The lawyer said MJM needed to be provided with copies of all relevant emails and that without them, it was ‘impossible’ to take instructions or to prepare a meaningful response. Deadline declined to do this for source protection reasons. ‘Bridgerton’ Season 3 Netflix The cases follow Deadline’s report in May that revealed MJM sent an actress self-tape auditions for roles in Bridgerton and Coronation Street , but she was later told that she was not called to audition for the series, and her tapes were not received by the casting teams. Jermin said the self-tape issues were due to an administrative error that had since been corrected. In a statement, Jermin’s spokesperson said: “Over more than 30 years, we have supported aspiring performers and their families through an industry that is highly competitive, subjective and often challenging. While individual concerns should always be listened to and considered carefully, we believe it is important that isolated incidents and disputes are viewed fairly and in their proper context. “We remain committed to operating professionally, transparently and in the best interests of those we support. We will continue to listen, learn and strengthen our processes where appropriate, while remaining focused on helping young performers develop and succeed.” If you would like to get in contact with the author of this story, please email jkanter@deadline.com.
